{{DISPLAYTITLE:Tactics}}
{{Technical|Lean theorem prover/System/The tactic framework|Lean theorem prover/System/Metaprogramming in Lean}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}

A proof in Lean can be written in two ways: as a '''term''', an expression whose type is the
statement, or as a sequence of '''tactics''', commands that tell Lean how to construct that
expression. This page explains what a tactic is, where the idea came from, which tactics are
met most often, and why no tactic has to be trusted.

== Two ways to write the same proof ==

In Lean a proof is a value, and the statement it proves is its type (see
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Propositions as types|propositions as types]]). Here is a
proof that "p and q" gives "q and p", written both ways:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
theorem swap_term (p q : Prop) (h : p ∧ q) : q ∧ p :=
  ⟨h.2, h.1⟩

theorem swap_tactic (p q : Prop) (h : p ∧ q) : q ∧ p := by
  constructor
  · exact h.2
  · exact h.1

#print swap_term
#print swap_tactic
</pre>

The first proof is a term. The brackets make a pair, and the pair is the second part of
<code>h</code> followed by the first. The second proof begins with <code>by</code>, which
switches to tactics. <code>constructor</code> splits the goal "q and p" into two goals, q and
p, and each <code>exact</code> supplies one of them.

The two <code>#print</code> lines answer with the same proof, word for word:
<code>fun p q h =&gt; ⟨h.right, h.left⟩</code>. The tactic script was a way of arriving at the
term. The term is what Lean keeps. Theorem Proving in Lean 4 calls the two styles
"term-style" and "tactic-style" proofs.<ref name="tpil-tac">Jeremy Avigad, Leonardo de
Moura, Soonho Kong and Sebastian Ullrich, ''Theorem Proving in Lean 4'' (online edition for
Lean 4.33.0, lean-lang.org), chapter 5, "Tactics".
https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Tactics/</ref>

== What a tactic is ==

A tactic is a small program that works on a '''proof state''': the list of goals still to be
proved, each with the facts available for it. A tactic either fails, or succeeds and leaves
some number of new goals, possibly none. When no goals remain, the proof is complete. Behind
the scenes, each step fills in part of the proof term, and each open goal stands for a part
not yet filled.<ref name="ref-tactics">''The Lean Language Reference'', version for Lean
4.34.0 (lean-lang.org, 2026), chapter 14, "Tactic Proofs".
https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Tactic-Proofs/</ref> How goals are shown and
filled is the subject of [[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Holes and goals|holes and goals]].

Lean 4's tactics are themselves Lean programs. Lean 4 is a reimplementation of Lean written
in Lean itself, and its users can extend it with tactics and decision procedures of their
own; many write their proof automation in Lean.<ref name="cade">Leonardo de Moura and
Sebastian Ullrich, "The Lean 4 Theorem Prover and Programming Language", in ''Automated
Deduction – CADE 28'', Lecture Notes in Computer Science 12699, Springer, 2021, pp. 625–635.
doi:10.1007/978-3-030-79876-5_37</ref> A new tactic can be an abbreviation that expands into
existing tactics, or a program that acts on the proof state directly.<ref name="ref-custom">''The
Lean Language Reference'', version for Lean 4.34.0 (lean-lang.org, 2026), section 14.8,
"Custom Tactics". https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Tactic-Proofs/Custom-Tactics/</ref>

== Where the idea came from ==

Tactics come from LCF, a proof-checking program begun by Robin Milner at Stanford in 1972 and
developed further at Edinburgh. In Edinburgh LCF the logic was set up as a protected type in
the programming language ML, so that theorems could be produced only by the rules of
inference. Strategies for breaking a goal into subgoals were ordinary ML functions, which
Milner called tactics, and functions that combine strategies were called
tacticals.<ref name="gordon">Michael J. C. Gordon, "From LCF to HOL: a short history", in
Gordon Plotkin, Colin Stirling and Mads Tofte (eds), ''Proof, Language, and Interaction:
Essays in Honour of Robin Milner'', MIT Press, 2000.
https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/~mjcg/papers/HolHistory.html</ref> Lean keeps the first idea, that
proof strategies are ordinary programs, and secures the second in its own way, by checking
the finished term, as described below. The history is told in
[[Lean theorem prover/History/LCF and the tactic idea|LCF and the tactic idea]].

== The tactics met most often ==

* <code>intro</code>: to prove "if A then B", assume A, give it a name, and prove B.
* <code>apply</code>: to prove a goal with a fact of the form "if A then the goal", switch to proving A.
* <code>exact</code>: finish the goal by giving a proof of exactly that statement.
* <code>rw</code>: rewrite the goal with an equation, replacing one side by the other.
* <code>simp</code>: simplify with a large stock of known equations.
* <code>induction</code>: split a goal about every value of a type into one goal for each way a value can be made, with induction hypotheses (see [[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Induction, as the machine sees it|induction, as the machine sees it]]).
* <code>cases</code>: split by how a value was made, without induction hypotheses. A proof of "p or q", for instance, was made either from a proof of p or from a proof of q.
* <code>omega</code>: settle a problem of linear arithmetic over whole numbers.
* <code>decide</code>: settle a statement by computing whether it is true.

The last two, with <code>simp</code>, are automation, treated in
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Automation and its limits|automation and its limits]] and
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Computation inside proofs|computation inside
proofs]].<ref name="ref-tacref">''The Lean Language Reference'', version for Lean 4.34.0
(lean-lang.org, 2026), section 14.5, "Tactic Reference".
https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/</ref> The first
three are enough for a short chain of reasoning:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
theorem chain (p q r : Prop) : (p → q) → (q → r) → p → r := by
  intro hpq hqr hp
  apply hqr
  exact hpq hp

#print chain
</pre>

The statement says: if p gives q, and q gives r, then p gives r. <code>intro</code> names
the three assumptions, and the goal becomes r. <code>apply hqr</code> uses the fact that q
gives r, so it is enough to prove q. <code>exact hpq hp</code> finishes: applying "p gives
q" to the proof of p yields a proof of q. Lean prints the term that the script produced:
<code>fun p q r hpq hqr hp =&gt; hqr (hpq hp)</code>. It is the same argument, read from the
inside out.

== Why a tactic need not be trusted ==

Whatever a tactic does, its product is a term, and the term goes to the Lean kernel to be
checked like any other. A tactic with a bug can fail, or produce a term that the Lean kernel
rejects. It cannot make Lean accept a false theorem. The Lean Language Reference puts it this
way: the worst a bug in a tactic can cause is a confusing error message, not an incorrect
proof.<ref name="ref-tactics" />

That is why tactics may be large, clever and written by anyone, including programs that
search for proofs on their own, while the part that must be trusted stays small (see
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/The small trusted core|the small trusted core]]). The
exceptions are visible. A tactic that rests on an extra axiom, such as
<code>native_decide</code> or the placeholder <code>sorry</code>, leaves that axiom's name in
the list that <code>#print axioms</code> shows for the theorem.<ref name="ref-validating">''The
Lean Language Reference'', version for Lean 4.34.0 (lean-lang.org, 2026), "Validating a Lean
Proof". https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/ValidatingProofs/</ref>

== Terms or tactics? ==

Neither style is more rigorous than the other; both end in the same kind of term. Tactic
proofs are often shorter and easier to write, and they open the way to automation, since the
automatic procedures are tactics too. They can be harder to read, because the reader has to
picture the goal after every step.<ref name="tpil-tac" /> A term shows the whole argument at
once but can be laborious to write by hand. In practice the two are mixed: a term may contain
a <code>by</code> block, and a tactic such as <code>exact</code> takes a term.
